content: Crypto exchange Gemini recently recorded a significant drop in its quarterly retail trading volume, hitting a three-year low. title: Sygnum Launches ETH Alpha Fund as Investors Look to Grow ETH Holdings Beyond Staking
summary:
Sygnum, a global digital asset banking group, today announced the launch of the Sygnum ETH Alpha Fund SP, giving professional investors a regulated way to grow their ETH holdings beyond staking. The market-neutral fund, denominated in ETH, targets annual returns of 8-10% in ETH, net of fees, and opened to investors on 2 November. 
Corporate treasuries and exchange-traded funds are now among the largest stakers of ETH, and staking rewards of around 2-3% a yearⁱⁱ have become the standard return on institutional ETH holdings. Building on this, long term ETH investors aim to increase ETH holdings without selling it or taking a view on its price. 
The fund keeps its core holdings staked natively with Sygnum, earning protocol rewards, and adds three further return sources, each with a different driver: premium from options, arbitrage between trading venues, and carry as well as funding rates in derivatives markets. These strategies are run by underlying managers who already operate them in other currencies, such as USD. All profit and loss is realized and reported in ETH, so investors grow the amount of ETH they hold rather than converting into dollar yield. As the fund is denominated in ETH, investors remain fully exposed to the ETH price, while the strategies themselves are market-neutral. 
“Institutions that hold ETH for the long term increasingly think in ETH, not dollars, and judge their year by whether they end it holding more. We built the fund around that measure, adding in-kind income strategies to staking within the safeguards of a regulated structure.” said Markus Hämmerli, Head of Asset Management and ETH Alpha Fund lead at Sygnum. 
With attractive subscription and redemption terms, a disciplined risk management framework and off-exchange safekeeping through Sygnum Protect, the fund is designed for professional and institutional investors seeking quality yield opportunities within an institutional-grade structure. The fund is managed by Sygnum Asset Management, a subdivision of Sygnum Bank AGs Investment Solutions department. 
The ETH Alpha Fund is Sygnum’s second alpha fund in just over a year, following the launch of the Starboard Sygnum BTC Alpha Fund in October 2025, and meets growing demand from investors for returns earned and paid in the digital assets they already hold.

title: The Rise of the ‘Pre-Prime’: Over 12 Million UK Adults Who Pay Every Bill on Time Still Turned Down for Credit
summary:
Millions of people are locked out of mainstream credit with no clear way in, according to Building Better Borrowers, the first Impact Report from credit-building and financial wellbeing platform Loqbox, published today.
Drawing on data from more than 291,000 members, compared with more than 300,000 similar consumers who hadn’t used Loqbox, it finds that when people are given an alternative way to demonstrate their financial reliability, they can build stronger credit profiles without relying on high-cost borrowing.
The UK credit system works well for those already established in it. But between four and five million people have little or no credit history, more than 16 million have experienced adverse credit, and many self-employed people earn in a way that doesn’t fit the pattern lenders expect. 
These consumers are usually labelled ‘sub-prime’, which describes where their credit file sits today and says little about the borrower they could become. Loqbox calls them pre-prime: people who haven’t yet had the chance to prove themselves, with many already doing the right thing. A new survey of 2,000 UK adults, commissioned alongside the report, found that nearly two-thirds (62%) have been declined for credit, a phone contract or a rental in the last two years, and more than a third (37%) of those say they paid every bill on time.
There’s also been a lot more focus across the industry on how people can build a stronger credit profile safely and effectively. Last year, the FCA published findings that questioned how effective certain credit builder products are for consumers.
The cost of getting started
For anyone starting out, the standard advice is to take out a credit card, use it a little and repay it every month. But the cards most readily available to people with little or no credit history are among the most expensive on the market. Almost half (49%) of UK adults have taken out credit they didn’t need just to build their score, and almost half of those (48%) struggled to repay it.
This is the price of the ‘first-rung premium’: credit builder cards average around 36% APR, nearly double the 18.9% on student cards. Yet nearly seven in ten 18-year-olds hadn’t secured a university or college place by results day this year, so for many young people, that cheaper option isn’t on the table. A product sold as a stepping stone can become a long-term cost, and the people least equipped to manage high-cost credit are often the ones most likely to be offered it.
What building better borrowers can look like
Analysis of almost 600,000 consumers revealed that members who paid Loqbox every month for a year, and didn’t miss payments elsewhere, saw their credit score rise by around 73 points on average. Comparable consumers who didn’t use Loqbox saw no increase. Among members new to credit, credit card holding rose from 15% to over 46% (against 22% to 29% for comparable consumers), while average balances stayed broadly stable at around £450.
When people can build a track record without carrying high-interest balances, they arrive in the mainstream credit market better prepared, gaining access without a build-up of debt. That’s what “building better borrowers” means: responsible access, rather than access at any cost.
Tom Eyre, Co-Founder and CEO of Loqbox, said: “Millions of people shut out of mainstream credit are managing their money responsibly and could be the prime customers of tomorrow. They just haven’t had the chance to prove it on paper. Our first Impact Report shows what can happen when they’re given a safer way to build a track record: stronger credit profiles, wider access to mainstream products and no build-up of debt along the way. The task is not to lower the standards for accessing credit. It is to give more people a fair opportunity to meet them.”
More than a score
The impact of a limited or adverse credit file goes beyond the score itself. Nearly half (43%) of UK adults say their credit history has delayed a major life milestone, including buying a home (21%), moving out (18%) or leaving a relationship (14%), according to the new survey.
For Loqbox members, the benefits go beyond credit scores too. Since 2021, over 370,000 members have saved more than £151 million, and 47% of surveyed members feel more confident about their finances.
Responsible behaviour often goes unseen by the credit system: rent paid on time, irregular but well-managed income, or a credit history built overseas. Declan Jarvis, a Loqbox member who moved to the UK from South Africa and works in finance, found he didn’t exist to lenders despite being a UK citizen with no history of debt: “Every time I checked, it just said I didn’t exist. I literally live here, but the system refused to acknowledge me. When I couldn’t pass a credit check for a flat, it suddenly felt really stressful, because I knew it would only get harder when it came to a car or a home. You assume if you’re sensible with money, it’ll all work itself out. It doesn’t.”
A better way in
Greater access isn’t always a better outcome. Credit needs to be appropriate, affordable and offered when someone is equipped to manage it.
That’s why Loqbox is calling for a better way in: an end to high-cost credit as the default first step, a restart of the FCA’s work on minimum payments, and updated guidance that reflects the range of ways people can now build a credit history and is clearer about the cost of the products most often recommended. The public agrees: 91% say people should be taught other ways to build credit besides a credit card, and 84% say people shouldn’t have to take on debt to prove they can be trusted.
By recognising progress, rewarding responsible behaviour and matching access to readiness, the industry can build better borrowers and give credit where credit’s due.

title: The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and the Bank of Thailand: Project Meridian FX APAC
summary:
The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and the Bank of Thailand today published the findings from their collaboration on foreign exchange (FX) settlement under Project Meridian FX APAC.
The project showed that synchronisation – a service that coordinates movements of central bank money – could be one approach to supporting interoperability across wholesale settlement environments built on different technologies and operating models. This marks significant progress in making cross-border FX transactions safer and more efficient, and supporting interoperability as different forms of money evolve in different ways. In light of the Bank of England’s plans to launch a live synchronisation interface in 2028, the findings provide valuable insight into how the approach could be developed into a live service.
Building on the earlier work, Project Meridian FX APAC tested payment-versus-payment FX settlement and multilateral net FX across the three central banks’ test environments, spanning both Real-Time Gross Settlement and Distributed Ledger Technology-based settlement systems. The project encompassed a wider range of currencies, technologies, infrastructures and time zones. Partior, the project’s delivery partner, developed, integrated and tested the Synchronisation Operator prototype for the trial.
The trial demonstrated that synchronised settlement can be achieved across central bank systems with different technologies and capabilities, while identifying the requirements and trade-offs involved. They also demonstrated how multilateral net FX settlement can support banks in using their liquidity more efficiently by netting payments against each other.
The project also examined the legal, regulatory and oversight considerations for applying synchronised FX settlement across diverse wholesale settlement systems. The analysis was informed by perspectives from the Reserve Bank of Australia and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, who participated as observer central banks.
The project’s findings and insights are published across three complementary reports: Introduction and Executive Summary, Technical Report, and Policy Report. Together, they set out the experimental results, key technical findings and policy considerations.
These results provide insights for further exploration of synchronisation as a means of enabling safer and more efficient FX settlement across diverse wholesale settlement systems. Future work could involve extending the existing approach to additional jurisdictions and industry participants, a wider range of currencies and transaction scenarios, and further consider the legal arrangements needed in practice.
Tom Mutton, Executive Director of Payments, Innovation and Fintech at the Bank of England, said, ‘Innovation has the greatest impact when it addresses real world challenges. Project Meridian FX APAC provides practical evidence of how synchronised settlement could help reduce risk and improve efficiency in cross-border FX transactions. The results provide a strong foundation for further collaboration as we explore how this approach could be developed towards real-world use’.
Kenneth Gay, Chief FinTech Officer at the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said, ‘Cross-border settlement increasingly takes place across systems built on different technologies and operating models. Project Meridian FX APAC has shown how synchronisation could help enable PvP settlement across these diverse environments, reducing settlement risk while supporting greater interoperability’.
Pucktada Treeratpituk, Director of Payment Systems and Financial Technology Policy Department at the Bank of Thailand, said, ‘Project Meridian FX APAC successfully demonstrated that synchronisation can work across diverse wholesale settlement systems, making cross-border FX safer and more efficient while preserving trust in central bank money. The insights on technical integration, operating models and regulatory considerations established a practical foundation for modernising wholesale settlement infrastructure’.

title: Rain Agent Vaults Bring Embedded Payments to AI Agents
summary:
Rain, the global payments platform for human and agentic transactions, today introduced Rain Agent Vaults, embedded payment infrastructure that lets an AI agent spend, receive, and send money from a balance its owner funds, within rules the owner sets. A vault is funded by bank transfer, card, or stablecoins, and the agent can only pay or send what is in it. Rain issues a scoped card for each purchase, accepted at 175 million merchant locations in 200 countries and territories, and agents can send funds to local bank accounts in more than 80 countries.
How Rain Agent Vaults work
Today, AI agents can search, compare, and shop, but paying remains a significant challenge. The options available to the companies building them have been a raw card number, which is a standing permission with no limit on what it can be used for, or a third-party wallet, which puts another company's login inside their app, that company's name on their users' statements, and one limit on the whole balance, set in that company's app. Companies enabling agentic experiences want their users to fund a balance once and never be asked again, and they want the relationship, the brand, and the payment to stay in their own product.
"People want to use AI agents that can move money as freely as humans do. An agent that can search for a new pair of shoes but cannot pay for them is not doing its job," said Farooq Malik, CEO and co-founder of Rain. "With Rain Agent Vaults, developers can build embedded payment solutions directly into their agents, giving businesses and consumers the ability to load a balance, set rules, and allow agents to pay in a trusted fashion. All of this is available in a single integration while the user, the rules, and the balance sit with the partner that built the agent."
Rain Agent Vaults are built for business and consumer use cases. Rain partners can embed agent vaults within their own apps and platforms, maintaining their own branding and customer relationship. A business can then fund an agent vault from its business bank account, enabling payouts to more than 80 countries around the world once specific rules and circumstances are met. Alternatively, a consumer can load funds directly into the agent vault from their card, set the rules, and a Rain-issued scoped card is created inside those rules for each purchase. The card information is then retired, preventing overspending.
For example, a bakery owner moves $5,000 into her bakery's vault, sets the rules so the agent may only pay suppliers and must ask her above $1,500, and leaves for the weekend. On Saturday the agent sees a run of orders for the week ahead and gets a card for $640 to buy 20 bags of flour from the mill. On Monday a catering order comes in and the agent gets a second card for $800 for 25 bags more. Both are suppliers, both are under her limit, and both go through. When the agent finds a mixer for $2,400, equipment is outside the rules, so the purchase is held for her to approve even though the money is in the vault.
Rain Agent Vaults build on the company's Agent Control Layer and scoped cards, which Rain partners already use to give agents real-world spending power. Rain started with stablecoin-powered cards and has grown into a full-stack platform where partners issue cards, run wallets, move money, and settle across card and blockchain networks through one integration. Every product a partner adds works with the ones they already run, so a balance that arrives by bank transfer can be spent by an agent on a card and paid out to a bank account in another country without a second vendor. Rain is a founding member of the Agentic Payments Alliance. Rain is enabling its programs for Visa Intelligent Commerce and Mastercard Agent Pay, so a scoped card issued from a vault will carry the networks' agent credential, which signals the user's consent to the merchant and the issuer, alongside the rules the partner set.

title: 86% of Financial Services Firms Use AI, but Formal Testing and Documented Oversight Lag, ACA and NSCP Survey Finds
summary:
AI adoption is widespread across financial services firms, and compliance teams are shifting their focus to assurance. According to the 2026 AI Benchmarking Survey by ACA Group (ACA) and the National Society of Compliance Professionals (NSCP), firms are increasingly focused on verifying that their AI tools perform as intended.
The third annual AI Benchmarking Survey found that 86% of respondents’ firms formally use AI, a 15-point increase from 2025 and a 41-point increase from 2024. Most respondents report using AI only for internal use cases. The survey found that 69% of firms limit AI to internal use cases, while 18% also use AI in client-facing applications. Nearly one in four are experimenting with agentic AI. Enterprise or private generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT Enterprise, Claude Enterprise) are the most widely used, with 85% of firms adopting these tools, compared with 18% using free or public generative AI tools.
The 2026 AI Benchmarking Survey was completed in September by 261 NSCP members and ACA clients. Across the three annual surveys, respondents’ focus has evolved from whether to use AI, to how to govern it through policies and committees, and now to how to test and validate it.
“Human review of AI outputs is increasingly common,” said Aaron Pinnick, Senior Manager, Thought Leadership, ACA. “But it must be supported by a disciplined approach to oversight, and with clear evaluation criteria and the right expertise. Without a disciplined approach, human review can become a procedural exercise rather than an effective control. Firms need to go further with formal testing, technical controls, and documentation that demonstrates effective oversight.”
Other key findings include:
Confidence in oversight is higher than the ability to document it: 81% of respondents agree or strongly agree that their compliance oversight is calibrated to the risk of the AI activity, but only 51% are confident they could produce documentation of that oversight on short notice.
Formal testing remains limited: 60% of firms have implemented human review of AI outputs on an ongoing basis, and 26% do so on an ad hoc basis, but only 38% have a formal program to test or validate AI outputs. Firms are aware of the importance of establishing formal AI testing programs. AI testing was the most common priority for compliance leaders over the next 24 months, and 24% of respondents are actively developing formal testing programs.
AI policies and training are widespread: Among firms that have adopted AI, 89% have policies governing employee AI use, up from 70% in 2025, and 66% have an AI governance committee or similar working group, up from 48%. Firms have also updated cybersecurity training (64%) and privacy training (65%) to address AI-related concerns.
Compliance teams are seeing value: 43% of firms use AI for at least one compliance activity, with firms using AI for an average of approximately three compliance tasks. Marketing and advertising review is the most common compliance use case: 41% of firms using AI for compliance tasks apply it to this activity. Among those using AI for marketing and advertising reviews, 90% report improved efficiency.
AI risk concerns are widespread, while technical-control adoption remains limited: Information security (68%), data privacy (59%), and cybersecurity (55%) remain respondents' top AI concerns, as in prior years. However, technical controls around AI tools that could help firms manage these risks are still inconsistently used by firms, with no technical control used by more than 36% of firms. Preparation for AI-related incidents and disruptions remains limited, but only 18% have an incident response plan that addresses AI-specific incidents and disruptions.
Enhanced due diligence of AI vendors is increasing: 55% of firms have enhanced their due diligence on AI vendors, up from 43% last year. As more firms rely on third-party AI tools, and these tools become increasingly integrated into operations, thorough vendor due diligence is important to managing AI risk.
“AI adoption and governance are top priorities for firms, compliance professionals, regulators, and investors. Today, however, if an examiner asks how a firm reviewed AI-assisted decisions and outputs, only about half of respondents felt confident they could promptly produce the documentation necessary to demonstrate effective oversight of AI,” said Carlo di Florio, President, ACA. “Although the SEC has not adopted a rule specifically governing AI use, firms remain subject to existing requirements related to fiduciary duty, governance, compliance, recordkeeping, vendor oversight, data protection, and other applicable obligations. Building testing and documentation into AI governance programs now will make regulator and investor conversations easier.”
“AI is no longer an emerging consideration for compliance professionals. It's increasingly part of their day-to-day responsibilities,” said Melissa Loner, CEO of NSCP. “What's encouraging is the progress firms are making in establishing governance frameworks, but this year's findings also highlight the work ahead in testing, documentation, and demonstrating effective oversight. Our continued collaboration with ACA gives compliance professionals valuable benchmarks to evaluate their programs, identify gaps and prioritize next steps.”
